items.title: ‘Voluntary, revocable’: The fine print behind Anthropic founders’ $112 billion giving pledge
items.summary:
Anthropic’s record-setting IPO may have created one of the largest pools of charitable capital ever assembled. Its size depends on a stock that has swung more than $30 a share in its first three sessions.

The Claude maker priced 980 million shares at $83 on Nov. 18, above its marketed range of $70 to $78, raising a record $81.3 billion and valuing the company at about $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis. The stock opened at $111.50 on Nov. 19, closed its first day at $97.17, then fell 8.5% to $88.91 on Friday.

On Monday, as the Nasdaq jumped roughly 6% on Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO, Anthropic went the other way. Shares closed down 1.4% at $87.64, about 5.6% above the IPO price.

What $156 billion looks like at $87.64 

TechCrunch estimated Thursday that Anthropic’s charitable commitments could be worth about $156 billion at roughly $95 a share, where the stock traded early in its debut. The figure combines the company’s Public Benefit Fund, employees’ pledged shares and Anthropic’s match on those pledges.

Because all three are paid in stock, the total moves with the share price. At Monday’s close, the same math yields about $144 billion, down $12 billion from Thursday. At the $83 IPO price, it would be roughly $136 billion.

Even the lower figures are enormous. By TechCrunch ’s count, Americans gave $617 billion to charity in all of 2025, so Monday’s value equals nearly a quarter of a year of U.S. giving.

Three channels on three different clocks 

The largest piece is the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund , a wholly owned LLC the company announced in…
items.t: ‘Voluntary, revocable’: The fine print behind Anthropic founders’ $112 billion giving pledge

items.title: ‘Doesn’t answer the big questions’: The stock market is still $5 trillion below its AI-fueled peak despite Monday’s rally
items.summary:
Wall Street’s full-blown gamble on the AI boom helped wipe out $8 trillion in stock market value before Jensen Huang’s return as CEO of Nvidia helped lead a rebound Monday.

Wall Street had its best day since April 2025 on Monday after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, 11 days after he resigned. The S&P 500 closed up about 5%, while the Nasdaq was up 6.5% and the Dow 3%, while Nvidia shares jumped 33% . Even so, the rally won back only about $3 trillion of the roughly $8 trillion the S&P 500 lost in the six weeks after its Oct. 6 record, leaving the index still about $5 trillion below its peak.

The swing shows how much of the stock market now rides on the AI trade. And Monday’s rally didn’t answer the question that started the selloff: whether the billions of dollars companies have poured into AI will pay off.

As of Friday’s close, the three biggest U.S. indexes had suffered steep losses with no relief in sight. The S&P 500, which tracks the broader market, was down 3.7%. Meanwhile, the tech-heavy Nasdaq and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 5.3% and 1.9%, respectively, with all three indexes wading into correction territory on Friday. 

The AI-fueled collapse of the last few weeks came after the S&P 500 reached a fresh record high on Oct. 6, when the companies in the index were collectively worth roughly $70 trillion . By Friday, just six weeks later, that value had plummeted more than 11%, erasing roughly $8 trillion in value , before Monday’s rebound.

The losses highlight how dependent the broader stock market has become on the AI boom. Of the top 10 biggest…
items.t: ‘Doesn’t answer the big questions’: The stock market is still $5 trillion below its AI-fueled peak despite Monday’s rally

items.title: DeSantis says a Florida city misread his anti-DEI law. Now a nonprofit needs $130,000 to save its St. Patrick’s Day parade
items.summary:
Delray Beach, Florida, had set aside about $77,000 for its St. Patrick’s Day parade, according to local reports. Now a local nonprofit says it will take $130,000 to run the event without the city, and its fundraiser has raised nearly $2,900.

The city has celebrated St. Patrick’s Day for more than 50 years with a parade of floats and marching bands that draw an average of 42,000 spectators, according to the city’s report for sponsors. But on Nov. 10 , Delray Beach announced it’s canceling the 2027 parade along with its Pride event because of a new state law officials argue makes it illegal to celebrate a specific group of people—in this case, the Irish. 

“Following a review of the legislation and its requirements, the City has determined that it is legally prohibited from organizing, funding, sponsoring, promoting, or marketing these two events in 2027,” a City of Delray Beach spokesperson told Fortune . “This decision is not budgetary in nature, nor is it the result of a local policy decision. It is a matter of compliance with state law, which applies to municipalities throughout Florida.”

The law is part of Florida’s broader crackdown on DEI—which has included restricting discussions of gender in public schools and ordering the removal of rainbow crosswalks—but its effect on Delray Beach shows how far its reach could extend: a measure targeting DEI is now being interpreted as a reason to cancel a celebration of Irish heritage that predates the DEI political debate. Now, the governor who signed it says Delray Beach has it wrong.

“Delray Beach is engaging in ‘malicious…
items.t: DeSantis says a Florida city misread his anti-DEI law. Now a nonprofit needs $130,000 to save its St. Patrick’s Day parade

items.title: ‘Superintelligence is arriving’: Mark Zuckerberg’s AI chief warns humanity may lose control as the AI bubble refuses to pop
items.summary:
Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer and the head of its Superintelligence Labs, posted on X on Sunday that “superintelligence is arriving.” He wrote that “the models are clearly going to be intelligent enough to automate all of AI research,” and that “it is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement.” He said the remaining obstacles are “no longer intelligence; they are domain-specific know-how, plumbing, and experimentation.”

“How humanity acts over the next year will have great consequence on what future world we live in,” Wang wrote.

Social media erupted over the latest warning from inside the AI thunderdome during a weekend when the AI bubble seemed to finally have popped — the day before it controversially reinflated again. Wang wasn’t even posting about Anthropic’s IPO or Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia and sudden reinstatement on Monday morning. 

He was riffing on just the latest historic math breakthrough with the help of generative AI: the claim by Levent Alpöge, a mathematician on Anthropic’s technical staff, of a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis made with Anthropic’s Claude . The 167-year-old problem about the distribution of prime numbers is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute’s $1 million Millennium Prize problems.

“It is hard to overstate the magnitude of discovery that we have just witnessed,” Wang wrote about the milestone, describing it as completed “with the help of an alien mind that we don’t understand.” He added that building an atomic bomb is “a homework problem…
items.t: ‘Superintelligence is arriving’: Mark Zuckerberg’s AI chief warns humanity may lose control as the AI bubble refuses to pop

items.title: Trump’s ‘assurance’ to Nvidia’s board over national security: protection from a major source of legal danger?
items.summary:
Ahead of Nvidia’s board of directors voting unanimously to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang less than two weeks after his ouster, President Donald Trump effectively gave them a major reprieve from some legal liabilities, one corporate governance expert said.

Trump told CNBC on Monday that Nvidia’s board “did ask for assurance on the national security threat,” seemingly referring to a White House guarantee that the board would be exempt from liability in an ongoing scandal over its former and current CEO’s embroilment in an international sex and espionage scandal. “And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know, and we know a lot.”

A White House spokesperson confirmed Trump’s role to Fortune : “President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board. We have to protect our geniuses.”

Huang, who cofounded the semiconductor chip giant 33 years ago, resigned earlier this month following revelations of an affair with a woman, Alice Huang, that U.S. intelligence that reportedly deemed a Chinese operative. Alice Huang is also an executive of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, which is being investigated for allegedly smuggling at least $7.5 billion of Nvidia chips . The Nvidia CEO also faces allegations of affairs with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, and a second unnamed Nvidia employee; it is unclear which scandal he resigned over, in fact.

Nvidia’s board reportedly met last Sunday night, just hours after Trump made a call on social media for Huang’s reinstatement .

Nvidia’s board may get a…
items.t: Trump’s ‘assurance’ to Nvidia’s board over national security: protection from a major source of legal danger?

items.title: AI startups feared Nvidia’s money would dry up without Jensen Huang. His return as CEO has put those fears to rest
items.summary:
Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO after just shy of two weeks of turmoil. The news—which has come as a shock to many in the tech world—was a welcome relief to the investors and Nvidia’s partners who had spent the majority of that time fretting that the company’s financial commitments might dry up.

Nvidia has become what some have referred to as the “central bank of AI.” The company has provided investment and supplied compute into various AI startups, neoclouds, and AI labs. These companies then, in part, use that money to buy Nvidia chips. Critics have called this process “circular financing,” with many saying it leaves much of the AI boom dangerously exposed to weak links.

Indeed as of the end of July, Nvidia had invested nearly $50 billion in AI model makers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI, and its equity stakes across the AI ecosystem totaled twice that. It has also pledged $170 billion of its investment-grade credit to help AI companies and neoclouds get financing.

Before news of Huang’s reinstatement broke on Monday, several investors and Nvidia partners told Fortune they were concerned that these commitments may stall under the interim CEO. That interim CEO, Colette Kress, some said, already showed early signs of being more hesitant to make deals at the same rate as Huang. Any new CEO, they added, would likely want to appear as a steady hand and more cautious when it came to spending. 

“Jensen has been such a critical part of the ecosystem because he’s allowed Nvidia to provide compute to venture stage companies who otherwise don’t have access to it,” said…
items.t: AI startups feared Nvidia’s money would dry up without Jensen Huang. His return as CEO has put those fears to rest

items.title: With Jensen Huang back as CEO, Nvidia’s SEC probe puts CFO Colette Kress in the spotlight
items.summary:
Following Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia , Colette Kress is no longer interim CEO. But as finance chief, a lingering Securities and Exchange Commission investigation could put Kress under scrutiny, raising questions about her future at the AI giant.

The Fortune 500 company announced Monday that Huang had been reinstated as president and chief executive officer and as a member of the board, effective immediately. He had stepped down on Nov. 12 amid reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman some officials believed was a Chinese spy. The White House told Fortune that “President Trump was totally involved” in Huang getting reinstated, and Trump said the U.S. government did not believe Huang’s return posed any national security risk.

“We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as Nvidia’s chief financial officer,” the company announcement said.

While the announcement indicated a return to Nvidia’s previous management structure, with Kress back in the finance chief role she’s held for the past 13 years, that may not be as easy as it appears. For one thing, it’s unclear whether the relationship between Kress and Huang has been damaged by the events of the past two weeks. And with Nvidia facing various investigations, Kress could be in the line of fire, depending on the outcome of the probes.

The SEC is investigating Nvidia’s accounting practices, Reuters reported last week. The Wall Street Journal previously reported the investigation, although its precise focus remains…
items.t: With Jensen Huang back as CEO, Nvidia’s SEC probe puts CFO Colette Kress in the spotlight

items.title: Billionaires spent $378 million to sink Prop 40. Norway’s 134-year-old wealth tax offers a different model
items.summary:
When Norway instituted a wealth tax in 1892, the U.S. was in the throes of the Gilded Age. American industrialists like John D. Rockefeller and Andrew Carnegie rocketed to unprecedented levels of wealth, while staggering economic inequality plagued the country.

More than 130 years later, Norway still levies that tax. And once again, the U.S. is experiencing an extraordinary degree of wealth concentration—by some measures, even exceeding Gilded Age levels.

The parallel now sits at the center of a live American debate. On Nov. 3, California voters rejected a one-time tax on billionaires even as they and voters in two other states backed higher income taxes on the rich . In Congress, Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Ro Khanna are pushing an annual 5% federal tax on billionaire fortunes. In Norway, a government-appointed commission recommended this year that the country cut its rate.

The two countries are working from very different blueprints. Norway’s tax reaches the middle class at about 1%. The leading U.S. proposals would hit fewer than 1,000 people at 5%. That difference shapes how much a wealth tax would raise, who would leave, and whether it would survive in court.

Norway’s model: broad, low, and modest 

Unlike the billionaire-centric levies that have dominated the U.S. debate, Norway’s wealth tax reaches a much broader slice of the population. For 2026, net wealth above NOK 1.9 million (about $197,000) is taxed at a combined local and national rate of 1% , with the threshold doubled for married couples. Above NOK 21.5 million (about $2.2 million), the rate rises to…
items.t: Billionaires spent $378 million to sink Prop 40. Norway’s 134-year-old wealth tax offers a different model

items.title: The Iran war drained U.S. missile stocks needed to deter China. The Pentagon has no overarching plan to restock, GAO warns
items.summary:
The U.S. military fields B-2 stealth bombers and Dark Eagle hypersonic missiles. What it lacks, according to the Government Accountability Office, is enough bombs, missiles, and torpedoes that wars actually run on, and an overarching plan to rebuild those stocks.

In a report released Nov. 19, titled “ DOD Munitions: Planning and Leadership Needed to Address Persistent Shortages ,” the GAO found that the Department of Defense has no overarching plan linking munitions production and funding to its total requirements. It also found that the department has not designated an office to lead the effort.

“A key part of military readiness is having a reliable supply of munitions, including bombs, missiles, and torpedoes,” the report’s summary begins. “But the Department of Defense has faced persistent munitions shortages.” The war the U.S. and Israel launched against Iran on Feb. 28 has made those shortages much harder to ignore.

The U.S. has fired more than 1,000 Tomahawk cruise missiles in the Iran war, according to estimates from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) reported by Axios . Using CSIS data, Fortune calculated in April that the U.S. had spent about $24 billion on seven major munitions in the war’s first seven weeks, and CSIS estimated it could take one to four years to restock them to prewar levels.

The consequences reach well beyond Iran. In its April analysis, CSIS warned that today’s levels “will constrain U.S. operations should a future conflict arise,” and that a war with a peer competitor like China would consume munitions even faster.…
items.t: The Iran war drained U.S. missile stocks needed to deter China. The Pentagon has no overarching plan to restock, GAO warns

items.title: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris
items.summary:
Last week’s Milburn review contained telling phrases, but the core problem is not Neets: it’s what capitalism as we know it has done to employment

Everyday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians about the UK’s serial woes and crises, one thing has revealed itself to me time and time again: the mess of cant, contradictions and tensions in our national understanding of work. Indeed, the higher up the hierarchies of power and influence any conversation about work goes, the more one vitally important subject seems to fall away: what paid employment actually is or ought to be.

All of this is reflective of a very British kind of amnesia. Of course poorly rewarded, unreliable jobs have always been part of our economy – and in the past a focus of fierce social conflict. But well within living memory a combination of the power of trade unions and the collective social conscience built into the postwar consensus resulted in an economy and labour market that now seem almost inconceivable. For sure they were scattered with restrictive practices and base prejudice: fathers securing jobs for their sons, people from minorities being excluded from work not just by people in management but by their fellow workers, and a great deal of…

items.title: The AI bust is a growing threat to China’s economy and a ‘moment of real danger’ for President Xi Jinping, analyst warns
items.summary:
U.S. investors are facing a meltdown in tech stocks and the possible end of the AI boom, but the bubble has already popped in China, where an even worse market crash threatens the economy and President Xi Jinping, according to Yardeni Research.

China’s tech-heavy STAR 50 index has tumbled 44% from its high this summer, while the Nasdaq is down 18% from its record—even after U.S. stocks suffered their worst week since the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic.

That’s thrown a wrench into Xi’s plans for the economy, Yardeni said in a note earlier this month. While the Chinese leader was riding high as host to global leaders this week, the market’s downturn jeopardizes his plan to turn China’s savers into stock investors who can finance the AI build-out and de-emphasize the property market.

Real estate accounts for roughly 70% of household wealth in China and was traditionally a place to stash savings. But the housing crash has weighed on consumer demand, even producing intermittent deflation. Business investment is also falling, with October data showing property investment sank nearly 22%.

With the domestic market still weak, Beijing has instead relied on a flood of cheap exports to keep the economy growing while also deploying the “national team” of state-backed banks to pump money into the stock market.

But according to Yardeni, Chinese stocks collapsed this year owing in part to cutthroat competition, heavier tax burdens, higher energy costs, tariffs, and the risk that China’s trading partners will block exports being sold at ultralow prices.

items.t: The AI bust is a growing threat to China’s economy and a ‘moment of real danger’ for President Xi Jinping, analyst warns

items.title: I hated life as a Neet. But now I’ve found a job, life is just as precarious | Emilija Morrison
items.summary:
The government’s plans to help young people not in education, work or training are welcome – I dearly hope they offer long-term security

  • Emilija Morrison is a University of Glasgow graduate and holds a Gold Standard NCTJ Diploma in journalism

What child dreams of being unemployed when they grow up? You can probably remember the days, aged 10, when you were asked to present to the class what you wanted to be. Imagine hearing this: “I want to be unemployed. After I graduate from university, I want to go to the jobcentre in my home town and collect my benefits every month.”

Yet that is the reality for many young people today – childhood dreams to become a teacher, a doctor, an engineer or whatever other profession thwarted not by the limits of their abilities, but the reality of the economy.

items.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
items.summary:
It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains

Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory.

Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage
items.t: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
